title: Supplementation with Akkermansia muciniphila in overweight and obese human volunteers: a proof-of-concept exploratory study
claim: A small randomized pilot trial reported improved insulin sensitivity with pasteurized A. muciniphila compared with placebo over three months.
studyType: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled human pilot trial
population: Overweight or obese insulin-resistant adults; 40 enrolled and 32 completed
limitation: A pilot intervention does not make genus abundance a treatment target or establish a patient's likely response. The preparation tested differs from naturally occurring stool abundance.

title: Akkermansia muciniphila and improved metabolic health during a dietary intervention in obesity: relationship with gut microbiome richness and ecology
claim: Higher baseline A. muciniphila abundance was associated with greater improvement in insulin sensitivity markers during calorie restriction.
studyType: Human dietary intervention with observational microbial associations
population: Overweight and obese adults undergoing calorie restriction followed by weight stabilization
limitation: Participants were not randomized to different bacterial abundances. Diet and the wider microbial community may contribute to the association.

title: A metagenome-wide association study of gut microbiota in type 2 diabetes
claim: F. prausnitzii and several Faecalibacterium gene clusters were enriched in controls compared with participants with type 2 diabetes.
scope: Species and metagenomic gene clusters; not all members of the genus
population: Chinese participants with and without type 2 diabetes
limitation: Case-control association does not establish protection or causation; diabetes and insulin resistance are different outcomes, and medication can confound comparisons.

title: Metabolic modelling of the human gut microbiome in type 2 diabetes patients in response to metformin treatment
claim: Two F. prausnitzii metagenomic groups decreased after four months of metformin, illustrating medication-dependent microbial changes.
studyType: Secondary analysis of human intervention metagenomes and computational modelling
population: Treatment-naive type 2 diabetes participants before and after metformin
limitation: Treatment context differs from untreated disease comparisons; these changes cannot be generalized to the whole genus or interpreted as worsening health.

title: A metagenome-wide association study of gut microbiota in type 2 diabetes
claim: Metagenomic clusters assigned to R. intestinalis and R. inulinivorans were enriched in controls compared with participants with type 2 diabetes.
scope: Species-specific associations: Roseburia intestinalis and Roseburia inulinivorans
population: Chinese participants with and without type 2 diabetes
limitation: These associations do not demonstrate that raising Roseburia improves insulin sensitivity, and a genus-level 16S result cannot identify these species.

title: Metabolic modelling of the human gut microbiome in type 2 diabetes patients in response to metformin treatment
claim: Roseburia sp. CAG:100 decreased after four months of metformin in this reanalysis.
scope: Specific metagenomic taxon: Roseburia sp. CAG:100
studyType: Secondary analysis of human intervention metagenomes and computational modelling
population: Treatment-naive type 2 diabetes participants receiving metformin
limitation: Medication-associated change is not evidence that lower genus abundance is harmful. Species and treatment context matter.

title: Human gut microbes impact host serum metabolome and insulin sensitivity
claim: B. vulgatus was one of the species driving an association between microbial branched-chain amino-acid biosynthesis and insulin resistance.
scope: Species-specific human association: Bacteroides vulgatus (historical name)
studyType: Human observational metagenomics and metabolomics study
limitation: The reported mouse challenge involved P. copri, not B. vulgatus. Neither a genus-wide causal effect nor an individual treatment recommendation follows.

title: Gut commensal Bacteroides acidifaciens prevents obesity and improves insulin sensitivity in mice
claim: B. acidifaciens administration improved insulin sensitivity in mouse experiments, showing that metabolic findings differ across Bacteroides species and settings.
limitation: Animal evidence does not establish human benefit and cannot be transferred to a genus-level stool measurement. This is context-specific evidence, not a direct contradiction of B. vulgatus findings.

title: Human gut microbes impact host serum metabolome and insulin sensitivity
claim: P. copri was one of the species driving an association between microbial branched-chain amino-acid synthesis and insulin resistance. Giving P. copri to mice worsened glucose tolerance and insulin resistance.
studyType: Human observational study plus mouse experiments
limitation: Human association does not establish causation. A genus-level Prevotella measurement cannot identify P. copri or its metabolic genes; mouse effects do not establish a treatment effect in people.

title: Dietary Fiber-Induced Improvement in Glucose Metabolism Is Associated with Increased Abundance of Prevotella
claim: After a short barley-bread intervention, participants whose glucose metabolism improved had more P. copri and a higher Prevotella-to-Bacteroides ratio. This illustrates how associations can depend on dietary context.
scope: Genus ratio and species-specific P. copri findings
studyType: Human dietary intervention with mouse microbiota-transfer experiments
population: Healthy adults consuming barley-kernel bread for three days; germ-free mice
limitation: Short intervention and responder comparison. The study does not show that increasing every Prevotella species improves insulin sensitivity, or that this pattern applies to the iPOP cohort.

title: Oral administration of Blautia wexlerae ameliorates obesity and type 2 diabetes via metabolic remodeling of the gut microbiota
claim: Blautia, especially B. wexlerae, was less abundant in association with obesity and type 2 diabetes in Japanese adults. B. wexlerae administration improved metabolic outcomes in high-fat-diet mice.
studyType: Human cross-sectional study plus mouse experiments
population: Japanese adults; mice fed a high-fat diet
limitation: Human findings are observational, and the intervention was in mice. A Blautia genus abundance cannot establish that B. wexlerae is present or justify probiotic advice.

title: Gut microbial carbohydrate metabolism contributes to insulin resistance
claim: A microbial group containing Blautia and Dorea was examined in relation to insulin resistance and excess fecal carbohydrates, illustrating a different context from the B. wexlerae findings.
studyType: Human observational multi-omics study with bacterial culture and mouse experiments
population: 306 adults recruited at health check-ups; diagnosed diabetes was excluded
limitation: Community-level associations cannot assign the same function to all Blautia species or establish that changing Blautia alone would alter a person's insulin sensitivity.

title: Ruminococcus bromii is a keystone species for the degradation of resistant starch in the human colon
claim: R. bromii breaks down resistant starch and can make starch-derived nutrients available to other gut bacteria in culture, offering a possible dietary-function context for this genus.
studyType: Bacterial culture and human fecal-community experiments
population: Human gut bacterial isolates and fecal communities
limitation: This is functional biology, not evidence that Ruminococcus abundance predicts or treats insulin resistance. Genus abundance does not identify R. bromii or measure starch fermentation.

title: Eight-week exercise training in humans with obesity: Marked improvements in insulin sensitivity and modest changes in gut microbiome
claim: An eight-week exercise intervention improved insulin sensitivity and was accompanied by an increase in the Ruminococcus gauvreauii group, which correlated with the insulin-sensitivity measure.
scope: Ruminococcus gauvreauii group, as reported by the study
limitation: Exercise has many effects; correlated microbial changes do not establish mediation. This small study's taxonomic group should not be equated with every feature labeled Ruminococcus.

title: Gut microbial carbohydrate metabolism contributes to insulin resistance
claim: A. indistinctus consumed several carbohydrates in culture. Administering it to high-fat-diet mice reduced intestinal monosaccharides and improved insulin-resistance-related outcomes.
studyType: Human observational multi-omics study with bacterial culture and mouse experiments
population: Adults without diagnosed diabetes; bacterial cultures and high-fat-diet mice
limitation: The intervention evidence is preclinical. An Alistipes genus measurement cannot establish the presence or activity of A. indistinctus or predict a benefit in patients.

title: Butyrate-Producing Bacteria and Insulin Homeostasis: The Microbiome and Insulin Longitudinal Evaluation Study (MILES)
claim: Higher Flavonifractor abundance was associated with lower insulin sensitivity and greater prevalence of dysglycemia.
population: African American and non-Hispanic White adults in MILES
limitation: Associations were adjusted for age, sex, BMI and race, but not multiple testing. This does not establish causation or individual clinical risk.

title: Taxonomic and Functional Fecal Microbiota Signatures Associated With Insulin Resistance in Non-Diabetic Subjects With Overweight/Obesity Within the Frame of the PREDIMED-Plus Study
claim: Odoribacter abundance was negatively associated with HOMA-IR, a marker of insulin resistance, in this baseline analysis.
population: Non-diabetic adults aged 55–75 with overweight or obesity and metabolic syndrome in PREDIMED-Plus
limitation: An association in this selected population does not establish that increasing Odoribacter improves insulin sensitivity or that it applies to all populations.

title: Gut microbiome and metabolome profiling in Framingham heart study reveals cholesterol-metabolizing bacteria
claim: Oscillibacter species were associated with lower stool and plasma cholesterol, and cultured human gut isolates metabolized cholesterol in laboratory experiments.
scope: Multiple Oscillibacter species; lipid metabolism rather than direct insulin-resistance evidence
studyType: Human observational multi-omics study plus in vitro isolate experiments
population: Framingham Heart Study participants and cultured human gut isolates
limitation: Cholesterol metabolism does not establish an effect on insulin resistance. Human associations and laboratory activity do not demonstrate treatment benefit.

title: Butyrate-Producing Bacteria and Insulin Homeostasis: The Microbiome and Insulin Longitudinal Evaluation Study (MILES)
claim: Pseudoflavonifractor was not significantly associated with insulin sensitivity or dysglycemia in the reported genus-level analyses.
population: African American and non-Hispanic White adults in MILES
limitation: A null result does not prove no biological effect. It provides useful context if this dataset shows an association; neither finding alone establishes causation.
